SQL and data modelling in one screen

About 45 minutes to read (the longest sections are joins, normalisation and migrations), plus the runnable examples and animations. Each numbered section can be read on its own. Numbers marked measured were measured for this page on a laptop (Apple M1 Pro, PostgreSQL 16.2 from the pgserver wheel); illustrative marks anything made up to show a shape.

SQL is how you ask a relational database questions; data modelling is deciding which tables, columns, keys and rules to give it so that the answers stay right as the product changes. The root page (Reading tab, section 2, and its SQL playground tab) teaches the first six clauses on the chat product's data. This page takes the same data from there to the level a professional backend engineer works at.

The data is the root's: 50 users, 200 chats, 2,000 messages and one credits balance per user. A table is a named set of rows with fixed columns; a primary key is a column whose value names exactly one row; a foreign key is a column holding another table's primary key (chats.user_id says which user owns a chat). This page adds one column, messages.parent_id: the message each message replies to (the previous one in its chat; empty for a chat's first message), so that threads can be walked in section 5.

The four tables and how they point at each other. PK marks a primary key, FK a foreign key; the arrow from parent_id back into messages is what makes a thread a tree.

Every grey box with a Run button is a real database. It is SQLite (an embedded SQL database that its authors call the most widely deployed database engine) compiled to WebAssembly and running inside this page, the same engine the root's playground uses. Next to its live result sits the result of the same query on a real PostgreSQL server (Postgres for short: the free relational database the root recommends as the default), recorded offline. Where the two disagree, the box says so: those differences are where real teams get bitten. Edit any query and run it; nothing you do leaves your browser.

The three ideas to keep
1. Write the query for the result, then check the rows: most SQL bugs return plausible numbers, not errors (a LEFT JOIN filtered in WHERE, NOT IN with a NULL, a join that repeats rows). 2. Put every rule the data must obey into the schema (keys, NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, foreign keys), because the schema is the only code every writer must pass through. 3. Change a live schema in small, backward-compatible steps with a lock timeout, because the dangerous part of a migration is rarely the change itself; it is what waits behind it.

Three tabs sit beside this one. Exercises lab has 28 graded exercises on this data, checked by the page's own database. ALTER TABLE, measured lists 21 common schema changes with the lock each took, whether it rewrote the table, and how long it took on a 2,000,000-row table. Further reading collects the sources.

1. How a query runs: written in one order, evaluated in another

The problem. You write SELECT first, so it is natural to think the database starts there. It does not, and that mismatch causes most beginner errors: an alias that "does not exist", an aggregate that is "not allowed here", a ranking you cannot filter on.

The idea. A SELECT statement is defined as a pipeline of steps, each producing a table that feeds the next. The PostgreSQL SELECT reference lists the processing order; every SQL database follows the same logical order:

The order you write

  1. SELECT (and DISTINCT)
  2. FROM, JOIN
  3. WHERE
  4. GROUP BY
  5. HAVING
  6. WINDOW
  7. ORDER BY
  8. LIMIT, OFFSET

The order it is evaluated

  1. FROM and JOIN: build the combined rows
  2. WHERE: keep rows whose condition is true
  3. GROUP BY: collapse rows into one per group
  4. HAVING: keep groups whose condition is true
  5. SELECT: compute the output columns, including window functions
  6. DISTINCT: remove duplicate output rows
  7. ORDER BY: sort (it can use output names)
  8. LIMIT, OFFSET: cut

The root page animates this pipeline on nine sample rows (Topic: databases, Reading tab, section 2). Four rules follow from the order, and each one is a common error message:

  • WHERE cannot use a name defined in SELECT, because SELECT has not run yet. ORDER BY can, because it runs after.
  • WHERE cannot use an aggregate such as COUNT(*), because groups do not exist yet; filter groups with HAVING.
  • WHERE cannot use a window function (section 4), because those are computed in the SELECT step; compute it in a subquery and filter outside.
  • LIMIT without ORDER BY returns whichever rows the engine found first. Without an ORDER BY, SQL promises no order at all, and the order can change when the data or the plan changes.

This first box already shows a difference between engines: SQLite accepts the alias in WHERE, Postgres reports column "doubled" does not exist. Write WHERE tokens * 2 > 1780 and both agree. The lesson generalises: test against the database you run in production; SQLite is a fine engine, but its dialect is more permissive.

NULL and three-valued logic. NULL means "unknown", not zero or empty. Any comparison with NULL (= NULL, <> 'US' when the country is NULL) is neither true nor false but unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. The root's playground has a NULL lesson (COUNT(*) against COUNT(column), IS NULL, where NULLs sort); section 2 shows the most expensive consequence, in NOT IN.

The logical order is not the execution order
The pipeline above defines what the answer must be, not how it is computed. The planner (the part of the database that chooses how to run a query) is free to filter before joining, use an index instead of reading everything, or stop early under a LIMIT, as long as the result is the same. How it chooses, and how to read its plan, is the Query planning and performance page and the root's Query plans tab.

2. Joins in depth

The problem. Normalised data (section 9) puts each fact in one table, so almost every real question needs rows from two or more tables at once: a chat's title with its owner's name, users with no chats, each reply next to its prompt. A join combines them.

The idea. A join pairs rows from a left table and a right table and keeps the pairs for which the ON condition is true. Read it that way, as "every pair, filtered", and every kind of join below follows. It is not a set intersection, which is why the familiar Venn-diagram pictures mislead: a left row appears once per matching right row, so zero, one or many times (Lukas Eder, "Say NO to Venn diagrams when explaining JOINs", jOOQ blog, 2016).

Seven joins on the same two tables

Five users (one with no country) and a small list of markets the company sells in (one market has no users). Pick a join; every output row is coloured by where its parts came from. Then add a market whose code is NULL and watch what happens to NOT IN.









Inner, left, right, full, cross


    

  • INNER JOIN keeps only pairs that match. A user with no chats disappears; a user with seven chats appears seven times.
    • 

  • LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN) keeps every left row; where nothing matches, the right side's columns are NULL. This is how you get "every user, with their chats if any". RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image; most people rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped.
    • 

  • FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides. It is the join for reconciling two lists ("which markets have no users, and which users are in no market?"). SQLite gained RIGHT and FULL joins only in version 3.39.0, 2022-06-25.
    • 

  • CROSS JOIN pairs every row with every row (no ON). 50 users and 200 chats make 10,000 rows. Useful on purpose for building a grid of every combination, as below; dangerous by accident (a forgotten join condition does the same).
    • 







The LEFT JOIN that silently becomes an inner join


Put a condition on the right table in WHERE and the NULL rows that LEFT JOIN kept are thrown away, because NULL = 'reasoning' is not true. The query still runs and returns plausible numbers. Conditions that should only limit what is matched belong in ON:




Self joins


A self join joins a table to itself under two names. With parent_id, each assistant reply can sit next to the prompt it answers:




Semi and anti joins: "has at least one" and "has none"


A semi join keeps a left row if some right row matches, without repeating it per match: EXISTS (subquery) or IN (subquery). An anti join keeps a left row if no right row matches: NOT EXISTS, or a LEFT JOIN keeping rows where the right key IS NULL. Writing a semi join as a plain JOIN repeats rows, the classic source of "why do I have duplicates?" and of a DISTINCT added to hide it:










Why. x NOT IN (a, b, NULL) means x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL; the last comparison is unknown for every x, so the whole condition is never true and every row is dropped. Two of the five team-plan users have no country, so the subquery contains NULL. NOT EXISTS asks a different question ("is there a matching row?") and is not affected. The Postgres project's own advice is blunt: "Don't use NOT IN" (PostgreSQL wiki); it also tends to plan badly on large subqueries. Use NOT EXISTS.


Fan-out: the join that doubles your totals


Join a parent to two different child tables (or to a child and a grandchild) and aggregate, and each parent row is repeated once per child row before the aggregate runs. Counts and sums come out too large, and nothing errors:




The rule: aggregate each child table on its own, then join the results (CTEs make this readable, section 5). COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) fixes a count but not a sum.


What a join costs
A join is work proportional to how the database finds matching rows: by looping, by building a hash table, or by walking two sorted inputs. Which one it picks, and why joining on an indexed column matters, is on Query planning and performance. One modelling consequence belongs here: Postgres indexes primary keys and UNIQUE columns automatically, but not foreign key columns; the documentation on foreign keys recommends indexing the referencing column yourself, because joins and deletes of the parent need it.






3. Aggregation: GROUP BY, HAVING, FILTER, ROLLUP


The problem. Reports ask for one number per thing: messages per model, tokens per user per month. GROUP BY collapses all rows sharing the grouping values into one row, and aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) summarise each group. Every column in the SELECT list must then be either grouped or aggregated; SQLite's leniency here (it picks an arbitrary row) is a lesson in the root's playground.


Several counts in one pass. A question like "per model: messages, replies, reply tokens, distinct users" needs conditional aggregation. The standard spelling is the FILTER (WHERE ...) clause, supported by Postgres and SQLite (see modern-sql.com's support table); in databases without it, write SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). One scan replaces four queries:




Subtotals. GROUP BY ROLLUP (plan, model) returns the per-plan-and-model rows, a subtotal row per plan (model shown as NULL) and a grand total (both NULL). CUBE and GROUPING SETS generalise it. SQLite has none of them, which is why this box is Postgres only:






Common aggregation mistakes
    

  • AVG of an integer column in Postgres is a numeric with many digits, in SQLite a float: round explicitly when you compare.
    • 

  • COUNT(column) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows. After a LEFT JOIN, count the right table's key, not *, or every empty group counts as 1.
    • 

  • Averages of averages are wrong when groups differ in size: average the raw rows, or weight by count.
    • 

  • SUM over zero rows is NULL, not 0: wrap it in COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) when a zero is meant.
    • 










4. Window functions: calculations across rows without collapsing them


The problem. GROUP BY gives one row per group, but many questions need every row and something about its neighbours: rank each user by tokens, the time since the previous message, a running total, the latest message per chat. Before window functions these needed self joins or correlated subqueries that were slow and hard to read.


The idea. A window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows, its window, and leaves the rows in place. Its OVER (...) clause has three parts:


    

  • PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups (each chat, each user). Without it, all rows form one partition.
    • 

  • ORDER BY orders rows inside each partition; ranking and LAG/LEAD need it.
    • 

  • The frame says which rows around the current one an aggregate sees: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means "this row and the two before it". If you give an ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW: from the start of the partition to the current row and every row tied with it (SQLite window functions; Postgres documents the same default).
    • 





Watch a window slide over chat 11


The messages of chat 11, in id order. Step through the rows: the frame (outlined) is what the function sees for the current row (highlighted), and the result column fills in row by row. Change the function or the frame and replay. The values are computed from the real rows.














Rankings. ROW_NUMBER() numbers rows 1, 2, 3 even through ties (so add a tie-breaker to its ORDER BY, or two runs can number tied rows differently); RANK() gives ties the same number and leaves a gap (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK() leaves no gap (1, 1, 2):




Previous and next rows. LAG(x) and LEAD(x) read a column from the row before or after. Time arithmetic is a dialect difference: Postgres subtracts timestamps into an interval, SQLite has no time type, so this box uses julianday there:






Two frame traps. First, LAST_VALUE with the default frame returns the current row's value, because the default frame ends at the current row; ask for the whole partition explicitly. Second, the default frame is RANGE, so rows tied on the ORDER BY value are all included at once: two chats opened on the same day get the same running count. Say ROWS when you mean rows:






Top N per group is the most common production use: number the rows per partition in a subquery, keep rn <= N outside (a window result cannot be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE, section 1). The root's playground shows "latest message per chat"; here, each user's two biggest chats. Postgres also has DISTINCT ON (user_id) ... ORDER BY user_id, ... for the N = 1 case.









5. CTEs and recursive queries


The problem. A real query has steps (aggregate messages per chat, then rank chats per user, then keep the top two). Nested subqueries hide the steps inside each other.


The idea. A common table expression (CTE), WITH name AS (SELECT ...), names a step so later steps can use it like a table. The fan-out fix in section 2 used two. What it costs: usually nothing. Since PostgreSQL 12, a CTE that is referenced once, is not recursive and has no side effects is inlined into the main query and optimised with it; MATERIALIZED forces it to be computed once on its own, NOT MATERIALIZED forces inlining (PostgreSQL 12 release notes; WITH queries). Older advice that "CTEs are an optimisation fence" describes Postgres 11 and earlier.


Recursion. WITH RECURSIVE lets a CTE refer to itself: a starting query (the anchor), UNION ALL, and a step that joins the CTE's previous rows to find the next ones, repeated until a step adds no rows. It is how SQL walks a tree or a graph of unknown depth: a reply thread, an org chart, a bill of materials, a category tree.






A third use is generating rows that do not exist in any table: every day in a range, so that days with no messages show as zero instead of vanishing from a chart. Postgres has generate_series for this; in SQLite a recursive CTE does it:




What it costs, and when not to
A recursive query on a cycle (a message that is its own ancestor through bad data) never ends: guard with a depth limit (WHERE depth < 100) or, in Postgres 14 and later, the CYCLE clause. Deep trees read many times are often better stored with a materialised path or a closure table (one row per ancestor and descendant pair); for traversals many hops deep across large graphs, see the graph section of NoSQL in practice.






6. Set operations, upserts and MERGE


Set operations combine the results of two queries with the same columns. UNION stacks them and removes duplicates; UNION ALL stacks them and keeps everything, which is cheaper (no de-duplication step) and is what you want unless duplicates are genuinely wrong. INTERSECT keeps rows in both; EXCEPT keeps rows in the first but not the second. All three compare whole rows and, unlike =, treat two NULLs as equal. Postgres requires an alias on a subquery in FROM; SQLite does not, another small dialect difference:




Upsert: insert, or update if it already exists


The problem. Count each user's tokens per day. The naive code reads the row, then inserts it if missing or updates it if present. Two requests at once both read "missing" and both insert: one fails on the primary key, or, without a key, you get two rows. This is a race condition (two operations interleaving so that the result depends on timing); the Transactions and concurrency page covers the family.


The idea. Let the database do both in one atomic statement: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET ..., where excluded names the row you tried to insert. It needs a UNIQUE constraint or primary key to detect the conflict. Postgres has had it since 9.5; SQLite copied the syntax in 3.24.0, 2018-06-04. MySQL spells it INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.




ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING plus RETURNING (which returns the inserted rows) is the standard way to make a handler idempotent: safe to run twice with the same input, as a retried request or a webhook delivered twice will be. The Building a backend API page builds idempotency keys on exactly this.




MERGE (SQL standard; Postgres since version 15) states several cases in one statement: update when matched, insert when not matched, optionally delete. It reads well for syncing a table from a batch. What it costs: unlike ON CONFLICT, a Postgres MERGE with both INSERT and UPDATE branches "does not guarantee that either INSERT or UPDATE will occur" when another transaction is changing the same rows, so two concurrent MERGEs inserting the same new key can fail with a unique violation; the MERGE page itself points to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT for that case. Use MERGE for batch syncs, ON CONFLICT for concurrent single-row upserts.









7. JSON columns and time zones


JSON in Postgres: jsonb


The problem. Some data has a shape that varies row by row and that you rarely query field by field: an LLM's tool calls and their arguments, a provider's raw response, user preferences, a webhook payload. A column per possible field would be mostly empty; a separate table per shape would be dozens of tables.


The idea. Store it as JSON in a column. Postgres has two types: json keeps the text exactly; jsonb stores a parsed binary form, so fields can be read and indexed without re-parsing. The documentation's advice: "most applications should prefer to store JSON data as jsonb". The operators to know: -> returns a JSON value, ->> returns text, @> tests containment ("does this document contain this sub-document?"), and a GIN index (a generalised inverted index: for each key and value, the list of rows containing it) makes containment queries fast. SQLite stores JSON as text with functions such as json_extract and, since 3.38.0, the same -> and ->> operators with a path syntax:




The last statement of the Postgres version shows the planner using the GIN index (sequential scans were switched off for the demonstration; at 2,000 rows a scan would be cheaper and the planner would choose it).




Use jsonb when
  • the shape genuinely varies, or belongs to someone else (an API response kept for audit);
  • you read the document whole, and filter on a few fields at most;
  • it is an attachment to a row that has real columns for everything you join, group or constrain on.


Use columns when
  • you join on it, group by it, or need a foreign key or a CHECK on it;
  • every row has the field (a "flexible" document where every row has the same keys is a table in disguise, without types or constraints);
  • you update single fields often (jsonb is rewritten whole on update).




The root's Database atlas compares this with a document database; the short version is that Postgres jsonb covers most document needs while keeping joins and constraints (Topic: databases, section 6).


Dates and time zones


The problem. A user in Tokyo asks for "today's messages". The server runs in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time, the time zone with no offset). Daylight saving time moves clocks in some zones twice a year. Times stored without saying which zone they are in become ambiguous the moment a second zone is involved.


The idea. Postgres has timestamp (a date and wall-clock time, with no zone) and timestamptz (an absolute instant). Despite its name, timestamptz does not store a zone: the input is converted to UTC and stored as UTC, and on output it is shown in the session's TimeZone setting (documentation). The same instant therefore prints differently in different sessions, while a plain timestamp prints the same digits everywhere and means nothing on its own:




Interval arithmetic respects the calendar: across the night New York moves its clocks forward, adding 1 day keeps the wall-clock time while adding 24 hours lands an hour later, and a wall-clock time that never happened is moved forward:




"Which day" depends on whose day. The chat data stores UTC wall-clock times in a plain timestamp (as many real systems do), so a per-user day needs two conversions, first declaring the value as UTC, then converting to the user's zone:




What professionals do
Store instants as timestamptz (the Postgres wiki's Don't Do This page says not to use plain timestamp for them); keep sessions in UTC; convert to the user's zone (an IANA name such as Asia/Tokyo, never a fixed offset like +09:00, which ignores daylight saving) only when bucketing by day or displaying; store a user's zone as a column if reports need their days. Use date for calendar dates with no time (a birthday). SQLite has no date type at all: store ISO 8601 text in UTC or integer Unix seconds, and be consistent.






8. Data modelling: entities, relationships and keys


The problem. Before any SQL, someone decides which tables exist. Get it wrong and every later query fights the shape: facts duplicated, relationships that cannot be expressed, keys that change.


Entities and attributes. Start from the nouns the product must remember, each with its own identity and lifecycle: a user, a chat, a message. Each becomes a table (an entity); its facts become columns (attributes). Then the verbs between them become relationships, and the kind of relationship decides where the key goes:




One to many
A user has many chats; a chat has one user. The foreign key goes on the "many" side: chats.user_id. This is most relationships.


Many to many
If chats could be shared, a chat would have many members and a user many shared chats. Neither table can hold the other's key, so a third join table holds pairs: chat_members(chat_id, user_id, role) with the pair as its primary key. The pair is the natural place for facts about the membership itself (the role, when it started).


One to one
A user has one credits balance: credits.user_id is both the primary key and a foreign key to users. Split one-to-one only for a reason: a different write rate (a balance changes on every message; a profile rarely), optional data, or tighter access control.




Which column is the key


A natural key is a real-world value that already identifies the row, such as an email address. A surrogate key is an id the database invents, with no meaning. Natural keys look attractive and age badly: people change emails, case and whitespace make two spellings of one address, a key copied into every foreign key must change everywhere when it changes. The production default: a surrogate primary key, plus a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key so duplicates are still refused. Join tables are the exception: their natural key, the pair, is the right primary key.


Which surrogate? Three serious options in 2026:


    

  • bigint identity (bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, the SQL-standard spelling Postgres has supported since version 10; the older serial is on the wiki's Don't Do This list). 8 bytes, sequential, compact. Use bigint rather than integer: a 4-byte integer runs out at 2,147,483,647, and changing a key's type later rewrites the table and every index (see the ALTER TABLE, measured tab).
    • 

  • UUID version 4: 16 random bytes (122 of them random). Any machine can generate one without asking the database, so clients can create ids offline, ids from separate databases never collide, and nobody can guess the next one. The cost: each new key lands at a random place in the index.
    • 

  • UUID version 7: standardised in RFC 9562 (May 2024), it puts the Unix time in milliseconds in the first 48 bits and random bits after. Generated anywhere like v4, but new keys sort after old ones like bigint. It reveals when a row was created, which matters for some public ids. PostgreSQL 18 (released 2025-09-25) has a built-in uuidv7(); on 16 and 17 generate it in the application or with a small function (the measurement below used one).
    • 





Why the order of keys matters: the same inserts into an index, twice


An index stores keys sorted in fixed-size pages (8 KB in Postgres; here each page holds 6 keys so it fits on screen). The same 36 inserts arrive in time order. With sequential keys (bigint, UUID v7) each new key belongs at the end, so only the last page is touched and full pages are left full. With random keys (UUID v4) each key belongs somewhere in the middle: pages split in half when full, and almost every page is touched. Illustrative page size; the measured effect on a real server follows.
















Measured: 1 million and 10 million inserts by key type measured


PostgreSQL 16.2 on a laptop, default settings (128 MB of shared buffers). For each key type, the keys were generated first into a temporary table (generation timed apart) and then inserted in generation order with one INSERT ... SELECT; the table has the key plus two integers. Choose the measure; the 1M figures are medians of 3 runs, the 10M figures single runs.












Reading the measurement. Two effects are mixed in it. A UUID is twice as wide as a bigint, so its index is bigger whatever the order. Random order adds a second cost: half-empty pages after splits (a bigger index for the same keys) and writes scattered over the whole index, which stops fitting in memory as the table grows and makes the write-ahead log (WAL: the record of every change, written before the data, which replicas and backups also consume) larger, because after each checkpoint the first change to a page writes the whole 8 KB page to the WAL (full_page_writes), and random inserts touch many more pages. Version 7 removes the second cost and keeps the first. What professionals do: bigint identity for internal keys is the simple default; UUID v7 when ids must be generated outside the database or merged across databases; UUID v4 only when unguessable, time-free ids matter more than write cost. If a public id must not reveal volume or creation time, keep a bigint primary key and add a separate random public id with a UNIQUE index.







9. Normalisation: one fact in one place


The problem. The tempting first design is one wide table: every message row also carries its chat's title and its user's name, email and plan, so any screen is one query with no joins. It works until a fact changes. The root page gives the one-line rule; this section makes it precise and shows what each step prevents.


The vocabulary. Column B depends on column A (a functional dependency, written A → B) if knowing A fixes B: user_id → email. A candidate key is a minimal set of columns that fixes all the others. An anomaly is a change the design makes easy to get wrong:


    

  • Update anomaly: one fact is stored in many rows, so changing it means changing all of them, and missing one leaves two versions.
    • 

  • Insert anomaly: a fact cannot be stored without some unrelated fact (in the wide table, a user who has not sent a message has no row).
    • 

  • Delete anomaly: removing one fact removes another (delete a user's last message and their email is gone).
    • 





One rename, two designs


The real messages of Ines Novak (user 7), one square per message row. In the wide table every square stores her name; in the normalised schema her name is stored once in users and each message reaches it through its chat. Play both: the same rename, the same buggy code path that only updates the chat she is in, the same question afterwards.








row stores "Ines Novak"row stores "Ines Novak-Reyes"row stores no name










The normal forms, by the anomaly each one removes


Codd defined the first normal form with the relational model in 1970, the second and third in 1971, and Boyce and Codd the stricter BCNF in 1974 (history summarised on Wikipedia). William Kent's four-page guide (CACM, 1983) is still the best short explanation. Each form adds one rule:




FormRuleA violation in the chat productThe anomaly it causesThe fix


1NFEach cell holds one value; no repeated groups of columns.chats.tags = 'sql,python', or columns tag1, tag2, tag3."Chats tagged sql" needs string matching; a fourth tag needs a schema change; no foreign key can check a tag.A table chat_tags(chat_id, tag), one row per tag.


2NFIn a table with a multi-column key, no column depends on only part of the key.chat_members(chat_id, user_id, role, user_email): the email depends on user_id alone.Update: an email change must touch every membership row.Keep email in users.


3NFNo column depends on another non-key column.users(id, country, country_name): the name depends on the country code; or messages(id, chat_id, chat_title).Update: renaming a country or a chat touches many rows; insert: no country without a user.A countries table; keep the title in chats.


BCNFEvery column set that determines another column is a candidate key.Reviews (chat_id, language, reviewer), each chat has one reviewer per language, each reviewer handles one language. Key (chat_id, language); but reviewer → language and reviewer is not a key.A reviewer switching language must be updated in every row, and a reviewer with no chats yet cannot be recorded.reviewers(reviewer, language) and chat_reviews(chat_id, reviewer).




Beyond BCNF, the fourth and fifth normal forms deal with independent multi-valued facts in one table (a user's languages and a user's devices stored as all combinations); Kent's guide covers them. In practice, a schema designed from entities and relationships as in section 8 is usually in BCNF already, and the forms are most useful as a checklist when reviewing a table that "has everything in it".


When to denormalise, and how to keep the copy right


Denormalisation is storing a derived or copied fact on purpose to make reads cheaper. It is right when a hot read path would otherwise do expensive work on every request, and you accept owning the copy. Every copy needs three things: an owner, a mechanism that keeps it in step, and a check that it still is.


    

  • Counters and totals on the parent (chats.message_count): kept by a trigger (code the database runs on every insert, as below) or by the application in the same transaction as the write.
    • 

  • Materialised views (Postgres CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW): a stored query result, refreshed on a schedule; stale between refreshes.
    • 

  • Read models and search indexes built from the change stream; the outbox and change data capture patterns are on Queues, streams and async work. Caches are the Caching page.
    • 

  • Analytics: wide denormalised tables in a columnar store, rebuilt from the normalised source (root section 5; Analytics: columnar engines, DuckDB and the lakehouse).
    • 





A copy that is not denormalisation
A snapshot of a historical fact is a different fact, not a copy: the price a customer paid (not today's price), the model that produced a message (not the chat's current model), the billing address on an invoice. Storing it on the row is correct normalised design, and looking it up "live" would be the bug.


Check that a copy is still right
A reconciliation query compares the copy with the source and should return nothing: SELECT id FROM chats c WHERE message_count <> (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM messages m WHERE m.chat_id = c.id). Run it on a schedule and alert on any row. The Exercises lab has one ("Find the impossible rows").






10. Schema rules: constraints, soft deletes, tenants, enums, names


Constraints are documentation that the database enforces


The problem. A rule written only in application code ("a chat always has an owner", "a balance is never negative") holds only as long as every code path, script, migration and teammate remembers it. The schema is the one place every write must pass through.


So the professional habit is to write every rule you can as a constraint. Each one also tells the next reader something true about the data, which a comment cannot guarantee:


    

  • NOT NULL on everything that must exist. Nullable should be a decision, not a default.
    • 

  • CHECK for value rules: CHECK (balance >= 0), CHECK (role IN ('user', 'assistant')).
    • 

  • UNIQUE for natural keys, and partial unique indexes for rules that apply to a subset of rows: "at most one pinned chat per user", "one live account per email" (soft deletes, below).
    • 

  • FOREIGN KEY with a deliberate ON DELETE: CASCADE (deleting the parent deletes the children: right for a folder's links), RESTRICT (refuse while children exist: right for anything with history, such as messages), SET NULL. SQLite enforces foreign keys only after PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON (SQLite docs); Postgres always does.
    • 

  • Exclusion constraints (Postgres) for "no two rows overlap": no two active subscriptions of one user with overlapping date ranges (documentation). PostgreSQL 18 added WITHOUT OVERLAPS primary keys and unique constraints for the same idea (release notes).
    • 







What constraints cost: a check on every write (small; a foreign key check is an index lookup on the parent), and adding one to a big live table needs care (section 11). Their absence costs far more: bad rows found months later, after reports were built on them.



Soft deletes and their cost


The idea. Instead of DELETE, set deleted_at = now() and hide those rows, so a deletion can be undone and audited. What it costs, as Brandur Leach catalogued in "Soft deletion probably isn't worth it" (2022):


    

  • Every query, report and join must remember WHERE deleted_at IS NULL; one that forgets shows deleted data.
    • 

  • Foreign keys stop meaning much: a live chat can point at a "deleted" user, and ON DELETE CASCADE never fires.
    • 

  • UNIQUE constraints break: a user who deletes their account and signs up again collides with their own deleted row, unless the unique index is partial (below).
    • 

  • The data is not deleted. Privacy law's right to erasure (GDPR Article 17) requires real deletion of personal data, so you still need a purge job.
    • 





Alternatives: delete for real and copy the row into an archive or audit table first (a trigger, or the application in the same transaction); or keep history as an append-only event table. Use soft deletes where users genuinely undo (a trash folder), with a view or row-level security policy that hides deleted rows by default and a scheduled hard delete after the retention period.



Multi-tenancy: many customers in one database


The problem. A business product serves many customer organisations (tenants). Tenant A must never see tenant B's rows, and one bug in one query is enough to leak.




PatternHowGood forCosts


Shared tables, tenant_id column ("pool")Every tenant-owned table has tenant_id; every index and key starts with itMany small tenants; the default for most SaaS productsEvery query must filter by tenant; a noisy tenant affects others


Schema per tenantSame tables in one Postgres schema per tenantTens to hundreds of tenants needing separationEvery migration runs N times; thousands of schemas strain the catalog and tooling


Database per tenant ("silo")A separate database or server eachFew large tenants, regulated data, data residencyCost and operations multiply; cross-tenant reports need a pipeline




For the shared-table pattern, Postgres row-level security (RLS) moves the tenant filter into the database: a policy attached to the table adds its condition to every query and checks every write, using a setting the application sets per request. Two details decide whether it protects you: superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS always bypass it, and the table's owner bypasses it unless you run ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY (documentation). So the application must connect as a role that does not own the tables:




Also include tenant_id in foreign keys (FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, chat_id) REFERENCES chats (tenant_id, id)) so a row cannot point across tenants, and lead indexes with it. With a connection pool, set the tenant with SET LOCAL inside each transaction so it cannot leak into the next request on the same connection (pooling is on Running Postgres in production).



Enums, CHECK lists and lookup tables


A column with a fixed set of values (a plan, a role, a status) can be declared three ways. A Postgres enum type is compact (4 bytes) and sorts in declared order, and a value can be added, but "existing values cannot be removed from an enum type, nor can the sort ordering of such values be changed" short of recreating the type. A text column with a CHECK (what the chat schema uses for role) is portable and easy to change. A lookup table with a foreign key is the most flexible: adding a value is an INSERT, and the value can carry data (a price, a label, a sort order, an "active" flag).






Rule of thumb: CHECK for small sets owned by the code (role); a lookup table when the values carry data or are managed by people (plans, countries); an enum only for sets that will genuinely never shrink.



Naming conventions


Names are read far more often than written, by people and by tools. The conventions most Postgres teams converge on:


    

  • lower_snake_case for everything. Postgres folds unquoted names to lower case, so a table created as "ChatTags" must be quoted forever (the wiki: don't use upper case names).
    • 

  • Tables plural (users, messages) or singular, but one choice for the whole schema. The primary key id; foreign keys <singular>_id (user_id); timestamps <verb>_at (created_at, deleted_at) as timestamptz; booleans as is_ or has_ predicates.
    • 

  • No reserved words (user, order, group need quoting); no abbreviations only the author knows.
    • 

  • Name constraints and indexes explicitly (chats_user_id_fkey, messages_chat_id_idx): migration tools and error messages refer to them by name, and Alembic cannot detect changes to anonymous constraints.
    • 









11. Migrations: changing a schema that is in use


The problem. The schema must change as the product does (a new column, a new table, a renamed field), but the database is serving traffic, several copies of the application are running, and during a deploy old and new versions of the code run at the same time. Edit the schema by hand and environments drift apart; change it carelessly and you lock a busy table.


The idea. A migration is a small versioned script that moves the schema from one version to the next, stored in the repository next to the code that needs it. A migration tool applies the scripts in order and records which ones ran in a table of its own (Alembic's is alembic_version), so every environment, from a laptop to production, reaches the same schema by the same steps. Two rules follow: never edit a migration that has run somewhere else (write a new one), and never change production's schema except through one.


The tools, as of October 2026




ToolStyleLatestNotes


AlembicVersioned scripts in Python, with autogenerate1.20.0 (2026-09-11, PyPI)The SQLAlchemy project's tool; compares your models with the database and drafts the script. Autogenerate cannot detect renames (it sees a drop and an add), so every draft is reviewed.


Django migrationsVersioned, generated from modelsDjango 6.1.1 (2026-09-02, PyPI)Built into Django; same review rule.


FlywayVersioned SQL files13.9.0 (2026-10-01)Plain SQL, language-agnostic, common in Java shops. golang-migrate (4.20.1) is the Go equivalent.


AtlasDeclarative: you write the desired schema, it computes the planv1.3.0 (2026-08-02)"Define your desired state, Atlas computes the plan"; also lints plans for destructive changes.


pgrollExpand and contract, automatedv0.16.3 (2026-09-08)Serves the old and new schema at once through views during the change, so it is reversible.


SquawkLinter, not a runnerv2.67.0 (2026-10-04)Flags migrations that take dangerous locks or rewrite tables; runs in CI. Rails has strong_migrations for the same job.


sqlcNot a migration toolv1.31.1 (2026-04-22)Compiles your SQL queries into typed code (Go, Python, Kotlin and more); it reads your migration files to learn the schema.




Versions read from PyPI and the projects' GitHub release pages on 2026-10-04.


Here is what Alembic actually generated for this page when the models gained a chats.pinned flag and the foreign-key index from section 2, followed by the SQL it would run (alembic upgrade head --sql, which prints instead of executing, the way to review a migration):


The SQL it emits


Notice what a reviewer must catch: the index is created without CONCURRENTLY, which blocks writes to messages while it builds. On a big table, edit the script to use op.create_index(..., postgresql_concurrently=True) inside an autocommit_block(), because Postgres refuses CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction.


Every ALTER TABLE takes a lock


Postgres protects a table's definition with table locks. An ordinary SELECT takes the weakest, ACCESS SHARE; an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE takes ROW EXCLUSIVE. Most ALTER TABLE forms take the strongest, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which "guarantees that the holder is the only transaction accessing the table in any way": while it is held, even reads wait. What separates a safe change from an outage is how long that lock is held, and the measured tab shows it for 21 changes. The short version, on the 2,000,000-row copy of messages:




    

  • Metadata-only changes take milliseconds: adding a nullable column, adding a column with a constant default (since PostgreSQL 11 the default is stored once in the catalog, not written to every row), dropping or renaming a column, changing a default, widening a varchar.
    • 

  • Rewrites hold ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole copy: a volatile default such as clock_timestamp(), a stored generated column, most type changes (integer to bigint, text to varchar(200)). Seconds here, hours on a big table.
    • 

  • Scans hold the lock while they check every row: SET NOT NULL, ADD CHECK, ADD FOREIGN KEY (which takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE: reads continue, writes wait).
    • 



Each slow form has a safe recipe: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (builds without blocking writes, slower, cannot run in a transaction); ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID (instant, checks only new rows) followed by VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (checks old rows under a lock that blocks neither reads nor writes); for NOT NULL, a validated CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) lets SET NOT NULL skip its scan (PostgreSQL 12 and later; PostgreSQL 18 also accepts NOT VALID on not-null constraints directly); for a volatile default, add the column nullable, backfill in batches, then set the default.


Older guides are out of date on two points
Many migration guides still say adding a column with a default rewrites the table; that stopped being true for constant defaults in PostgreSQL 11 (2018), and the measurement agrees ( ms on 2,000,000 rows). GoCardless's widely shared "Zero-downtime Postgres migrations: the hard parts" was written against PostgreSQL 9.4 (its footnotes say so) and says adding a foreign key takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks on both tables. PostgreSQL 9.5 reduced the lock level of foreign key commands; current Postgres takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on both tables, which was measured here: reads continue, writes wait. Its central lesson, the lock queue below, is still exactly right.


The lock queue: how a 1 ms change causes an outage


Locks are granted in order. If a long transaction holds even the weakest lock on a table (a report running a slow SELECT, or a request that opened a transaction and is waiting on a model call), an ALTER TABLE asking for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE must wait for it. Worse, every query that arrives after the ALTER queues behind it, because granting them would starve the ALTER. A change that would take a millisecond blocks all traffic to the table for as long as the oldest transaction lasts. The animation replays three real runs on the 2,000,000-row table: one long transaction holding the table for 4 seconds, one ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT 0 (metadata only), and seven ordinary point reads arriving every half second.










long transactionALTER waiting, then doneALTER attempt that gave upread that waited over 100 msread served at once










The fix is to bound the wait, not to hope. Set lock_timeout in every migration session (SET lock_timeout = '500ms'): the ALTER gives up instead of queueing indefinitely (documentation), and the migration retries with a pause. Readers then wait at most the timeout. Set statement_timeout on backfills, keep application transactions short, and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so a forgotten open transaction cannot hold locks forever.


Expand and contract: changes that never break running code


During a rolling deploy, old and new versions of the application run at the same time, so every intermediate schema must work with both. Expand and contract (also called parallel change) splits a breaking change into backward-compatible steps, each deployed on its own. Renaming chats.title to chats.name:


    

  1. Expand: ALTER TABLE chats ADD COLUMN name text (metadata only).
    2. 

  2. Write both: deploy code that writes title and name (or add a trigger that copies one to the other).
    3. 

  3. Backfill in batches: UPDATE chats SET name = title WHERE id BETWEEN $1 AND $2 AND name IS NULL, a few thousand rows per transaction, with a pause between batches, so no lock or replication lag builds up.
    4. 

  4. Read the new column: deploy code that reads name.
    5. 

  5. Stop writing the old one once no running version reads it.
    6. 

  6. Contract: ALTER TABLE chats DROP COLUMN title, a release or more later.
    7. 



Each step can be rolled back by redeploying the previous code. RENAME COLUMN itself is instant, but it breaks every running instance that still uses the old name; that, not the lock, is why renames go through these six steps.


What professionals do
Migrations in the repository, applied by CI/CD (continuous integration and delivery: automated testing and deployment) before the code that needs them; reviewed as SQL, not just as model diffs; linted (Squawk, strong_migrations); timed on a production-sized copy; run with lock_timeout and retries; one risky operation per migration; roll forward with a new migration rather than run "down" migrations in production, with backups and point-in-time recovery as the real safety net (Running Postgres in production).






12. ORMs against raw SQL, and the N+1 query problem


The problem. Application code works with objects (a Chat with a list of Messages); the database works with rows. Writing the SQL and the conversion by hand for every screen is repetitive and easy to get subtly wrong.


The idea. An ORM (object-relational mapper) maps tables to classes and rows to objects, writes the SQL for you, and tracks changes to objects so it can save them. In Python the standard is SQLAlchemy (2.1.3, released 2026-10-03 per PyPI); its 2.x style declares typed models and builds queries with select(). These are the models the measurement below used, mapped onto the existing chat tables:


class Chat(Base):
    __tablename__ = "chats"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"))
    title: Mapped[str | None]
    created_at: Mapped[datetime.datetime]
    messages: Mapped[list["Message"]] = relationship(order_by="Message.id")

chats = session.scalars(select(Chat).order_by(Chat.created_at.desc()).limit(50)).all()
for c in chats:
    print(c.id, len(c.messages))      # each c.messages here is a new query


What an ORM gives you: less boilerplate for create, read, update and delete; queries composed from Python pieces; parameters bound safely by default (section 13); an identity map (one object per row per session) and a unit of work (changes flushed in a valid order); and models that Alembic can diff. What it costs: the SQL and, above all, the number of round trips to the database are hidden. A round trip is one request and its reply over the network; inside one data centre it is a fraction of a millisecond to a millisecond or two, and it is paid per query, however small the query.


The N+1 query problem. The loop above runs 1 query for the chats and then, because relationships load lazily by default (only when first touched), 1 more query per chat: N+1 in total. The SQLAlchemy documentation names it as "one of the most common issues referred to in object relational mapping". It is invisible in development, where the database is on the same machine and there are ten rows, and it grows linearly with the page size and the network distance. Measured for this page:




Four ways to load N chats with their messages measured


PostgreSQL 16.2, SQLAlchemy 2.1.3, psycopg 3.3.6, the chat data with an index on messages.chat_id. Each bar is the median of 30 runs of "load the N most recent chats, with each one's message count and last message"; every SQL statement sent was counted. "Through 1 ms of network" sends the same traffic through a small proxy that adds 0.5 ms each way, about the round trip between two machines in one region. All four return identical results.
















The fixes, in SQLAlchemy
    

  • selectinload(Chat.messages): a second query WHERE chat_id IN (...) loads all the children at once; 2 queries whatever N. The documentation calls it "the most simple and efficient way to eagerly load collections".
    • 

  • joinedload(Chat.messages): one query with a LEFT JOIN; each chat's columns repeat once per message, so it suits many-to-one (a message's chat) better than one-to-many.
    • 

  • raiseload("*") in tests or on hot paths turns any accidental lazy load into an error, so N+1 cannot creep back.
    • 

  • Or write the query: one SQL statement that aggregates in the database returns only what the screen needs.
    • 



What professionals do
    

  • ORM for ordinary reads and writes; hand-written SQL (SQLAlchemy Core, text(), or sqlc) for reports and anything performance-critical.
    • 

  • Look at the SQL: create_engine(..., echo=True) in development, and per-request query counts in tracing (Observability).
    • 

  • Assert query counts in tests for important endpoints.
    • 

  • Paginate by key, not by OFFSET (Building a backend API measures why).
    • 










13. SQL injection and parameterised queries


The problem. If a program builds SQL by pasting user input into the query text, the input can change the query's meaning. That is SQL injection, still near the top of the OWASP list of web risks. The demo below is a real "find my account" lookup running in the page's database; try the inputs.









String concatenation


Bound parameter








The fix: parameterised queries. Write the query with placeholders (? in SQLite, %s in psycopg, :name in SQLAlchemy's text()) and pass the values separately. The value is then data, never SQL, whatever it contains; an apostrophe in a real name stops being a bug too. Psycopg 3 goes further and "sends the query and the parameters to the server separately"; its documentation's rule is "Never use % or + to merge values into queries".


# wrong: the input becomes part of the SQL
cur.execute(f"SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'")
# right: the input is a value
cur.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,))
# SQLAlchemy
session.execute(text("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = :e"), {"e": email})


    

  • Identifiers cannot be parameters. A table name, a column to sort by or ASC/DESC from user input must come from an allow-list in your code, or be quoted with psycopg.sql.Identifier (psycopg.sql).
    • 

  • An ORM protects you only while you use it as intended: text() or raw SQL built with f-strings is as vulnerable as anything else.
    • 

  • Defence in depth: the application's database role gets only the privileges it needs (no DDL, no superuser), and row-level security (section 10) limits what a successful injection could read.
    • 

  • LLM-written SQL (text-to-SQL features, agents with a database tool) is untrusted input of the same kind: run it as a read-only role, with row-level security, a statement_timeout and a row limit, never as the application's owner role.
    • 








14. Common mistakes, and the habits that prevent them




A LEFT JOIN filtered in WHERE
Turns into an inner join and drops the rows you kept on purpose. Put conditions on the right table in ON (section 2).


NOT IN over a column that can be NULL
Returns no rows at all. Use NOT EXISTS (section 2).


Aggregating across two joined child tables
Fan-out multiplies counts and sums. Aggregate each child on its own, then join (section 2).


LIMIT without ORDER BY, or ROW_NUMBER without a tie-breaker
The rows you get can change between runs. Order by something unique (section 1, section 4).


Window frames left to the default
LAST_VALUE returns the current row; RANGE includes ties. Write the frame you mean (section 4).


Read, then insert or update, in application code
Races under concurrency. Use one atomic INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (section 6).


Plain timestamp for instants, fixed offsets for zones
Ambiguous times and wrong day boundaries twice a year. timestamptz, IANA zone names, convert at the edges (section 7).


A natural key (email) as the primary key; integer instead of bigint
Keys that change or run out. Surrogate bigint or UUID v7 plus UNIQUE on the natural key (section 8).


Copying facts without an owner
Denormalised copies drift. Every copy needs a sync mechanism and a reconciliation query (section 9).


Rules only in application code; unindexed foreign keys
Put rules in the schema; index the referencing column of every foreign key you join on or delete through (sections 2 and 10).


Soft deletes everywhere by default
Leaks deleted data, breaks unique constraints and foreign keys, and does not erase anything. Use them only where users undo, with a partial unique index and a purge job (section 10).


A migration without lock_timeout; an index built without CONCURRENTLY
A queued ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock blocks every query behind it; a plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes. Bound the wait and use the non-blocking forms (section 11 and the ALTER TABLE tab).


Renaming or dropping a column in one step
Breaks the old code still running during the deploy. Expand and contract (section 11).


Lazy loading in a loop
N+1 queries; at 200 rows over 1 ms of network, measured at hundreds of milliseconds. selectinload, raiseload in tests, or one SQL query (section 12).


Building SQL with string formatting
Injection, and broken queries for names with apostrophes. Bound parameters; allow-lists for identifiers (section 13).


Testing on SQLite, running on Postgres
The dialects differ in ways that matter (aliases in WHERE, loose GROUP BY, foreign keys off by default, typing). Test against the production engine; run Postgres in a container or with pgserver in CI.




The habits, in one list
Write the expected result before the query, then check the rows, not just that it ran. Name things consistently. Every rule you can in the schema. Every schema change through a reviewed, linted, timed migration with a lock timeout. Look at the SQL your ORM sends and count it. Bind every value. Test on the engine you run. Then, when it is correct, make it fast: Query planning and performance and Transactions and concurrency are the next pages.

ALTER TABLE, measured: what each schema change locks, rewrites and costs


Twenty-one common schema changes, each run on a copy of the chat messages grown to  rows ( of table data) on PostgreSQL 16.2, with what it actually did.


How it was measured (src/pg/measure_alter.py): each change ran inside its own transaction; while that transaction was still open, pg_locks was read for the locks it held on the table, and a second session tried a point SELECT and an INSERT with lock_timeout = 300ms to see whether they were blocked; the table's file node was compared before and after to see whether the table was rewritten; then the transaction was rolled back so every change started from the same table. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction, so it was watched from a second session while it ran. Times are medians of 3 runs on a laptop. Lock names: AccessExclusive blocks everything, reads included; ShareRowExclusive and Share block writes but not reads; ShareUpdateExclusive blocks neither, only other schema changes and VACUUM (PostgreSQL table-level locks).












Read the times in context
A metadata-only change finishes in about a millisecond whatever the table size; the danger is the lock queue in front of it (Reading, section 11). A rewrite or a scan grows with the table: the "your table" column scales the measured time linearly with the row count, which is a rough guide only (it ignores memory, disk speed, indexes and concurrent load). Plan with a measurement on a production-sized copy.

Data modelling




Kent, A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms (CACM, 1983)
Every normal form with one example each, in four pages. 20 min


Codd, A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (CACM, 1970)
The paper that started it; section 1 is readable today. 45 min


PostgreSQL wiki: Don't Do This
NOT IN, plain timestamp, serial, upper-case names, money, varchar(n) and more, each with why and when it is fine. 25 min


RFC 9562: UUIDs (May 2024)
Read section 5.4 (v4), 5.7 (v7) and 6 (best practices). 25 min


Brandur Leach, Soft deletion probably isn't worth it (2022)
The costs of deleted_at, and the deleted-records table alternative. 10 min


PostgreSQL: row security policies
Policies, USING against WITH CHECK, who bypasses them. 20 min


Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications
Chapter 2 (data models and query languages) puts relational, document and graph models side by side. 1.5 hours




Migrations




PostgreSQL: explicit locking
The table of lock modes and what each conflicts with; which command takes which. 20 min


PostgreSQL: ALTER TABLE (Notes)
Which forms rewrite, which scan, NOT VALID and VALIDATE. 20 min


GoCardless, Zero-downtime Postgres migrations: the hard parts
The lock queue outage, told from production (written for 9.4; see the correction box in section 11). 15 min


strong_migrations README
A catalogue of dangerous operations and the safe way to do each; useful whatever your language. 25 min


Squawk rules
The checks a migration linter runs, each with its reason. 20 min


Alembic tutorial
Setting up migrations for a SQLAlchemy project; then the autogenerate page. 40 min




ORMs and safety




SQLAlchemy ORM quick start
Models, sessions and select() in the 2.x style used in section 12. 30 min


SQLAlchemy: relationship loading techniques
Lazy, selectin, joined and raise loading, and when to use each. 30 min


OWASP SQL injection prevention cheat sheet
Parameterised queries first, then allow-lists, least privilege. 20 min


psycopg 3: passing parameters to SQL queries
Placeholders, the rules, and psycopg.sql for identifiers. 15 min




Built from src/: the examples were run on PostgreSQL 16.2 (pgserver wheel) and SQLite on 2026-10-04; the in-page engine is sql.js 1.14.2 (MIT; SQLite is public domain), shared with the root page. Reproduce with the commands in src/README.md.
